opportunities.title: 24/7 Breakdown Intake & Dispatch Agent (after-hours triage that never misses a call)
opportunities.problem: AMEC advertises 24/7 breakdown service for uptime-critical clients (server rooms, refrigerated warehouses, food processing) but delivers it through rotating on-call duty among field staff, coordinated by five supervisors, behind one published main phone number. There is no separate emergency web path, no callback automation, no escalation logic and no visible dispatch system. Every after-hours breakdown therefore depends on a human answering, working out which tech is on call, and relaying address, equipment and access details by phone.
evidence: Home page and contact page promise 24/7 breakdown service but publish only the main office number (732) 205-1507 as the emergency line, with no separate after-hours route — https://www.amecelectric.com/contact

Company feature describes 24/7 service run by employees rotating on-call duty, driving company vans home to go straight to jobs, coordinated by supervisors who 'look ahead, solve problems, build a plan' — i.e. dispatch is supervisor human judgment, not a system — https://www.amecelectric.com/assets/docs/creating-connections.pdf

Web intake is a form asking name, work email, phone, company, service dropdown and project details; the site states AMEC staff will review it and follow up on service, scheduling or quote information, so no instant acknowledgement or self-scheduling exists — https://www.amecelectric.com/free-consultation
No booking widget, chat or customer portal is present anywhere on the site; the only self-service login is employees-only with a single shared password — https://www.amecelectric.com/employees
Triage of a fault by phone before a truck rolls is a documented core task for trade technicians — https://www.onetonline.org/link/summary/49-9021.00

Measured analogue: a generative-AI assistant raised issues resolved per hour by 14% across 5,179 customer-support agents (34% for novices); the industry brief labels this peer-reviewed and flags it as the closest large-scale measured analogue to a contractor's booking/dispatch desk — https://www.nber.org/papers/w31161
opportunities.agent_design: An always-on intake agent sits in front of the main number and the web/email forms. Triggers: inbound call (voice agent with speech-to-text), inbound email, web-form submission, or an SMS from a known facility contact. On trigger it captures site address, contact, equipment/panel ID, symptom, safety flags (live panel, water, refrigeration temperature loss), and urgency tier; it looks up the account in the work-ticket data, resolves which technician is on call this week from the rotation roster, and drafts a work ticket plus a dispatch proposal. Systems touched: telephony/IVR, email inbox, web form endpoint, the internal work-ticket tool, the on-call rotation sheet, Google Calendar-style availability, and SMS to the tech. Human approval: the on-call supervisor receives a one-tap approve/edit on any dispatch decision and is the only path to committing a truck; low-urgency requests are queued for morning review by the office manager. Hard rules: the agent never quotes a price, never promises an arrival time it cannot verify against the roster, and escalates immediately to a human if no on-call tech acknowledges within a set window.
opportunities.why_not_DIY: This is not a chatbot bolted onto the website. It has to answer a live phone line at 2am, hold state across voice/SMS/email, read and write an internal work-ticket tool that has no public API, join against a rotation roster that changes weekly, and then hand a supervisor a decision with an audit trail. Reliability matters more than fluency: a dropped emergency call to a refrigeration or server-room client is a lost account, not a bad demo. Voice latency, telephony provisioning, consent/recording handling and fallback-to-human logic all have to be engineered and monitored, which is ongoing AgentOps work rather than a subscription.

impact_estimate.range: $16,000–$44,000/yr of recovered supervisory and office time, plus unquantified avoided lost emergency jobs
impact_estimate.assumptions: Assumes five field supervisors each spend 3–5 hrs/week on after-hours call pickup, triage and dispatch relay (15–25 hrs/week total). Valued at the NJ median for First-Line Supervisors of Construction Trades and Extraction Workers ($105,510/yr ≈ $50.73/hr) → 780–1,300 hrs/yr ≈ $40k–$66k of supervisory time at full rate. The pilot is assumed to absorb 40–65% of that relay work → $16k–$44k. Deliberately excluded from the range: revenue from emergency jobs that currently go unanswered or to a competitor — ticket size and call volume are not public, so that upside is stated as unquantified rather than estimated. Range is mid-point conservative because supervisors will still own the approve/edit decision.

opportunities.pilot_scope: 2–4 weeks: instrument one phone line and the web form; build the triage schema and safety/urgency tiers; connect read-only to the work-ticket tool and the on-call roster; run the agent in shadow mode alongside staff for the first two weeks and log what it would have dispatched versus what a supervisor actually did; then enable supervisor-approved dispatch for after-hours calls only, with a written escalation SLA and a weekly accuracy review.

opportunities.title: Quote & Bid Intake Agent — RFQ to estimate-ready package, routed to the Senior Estimator
opportunities.problem: Every quote request — whether it arrives by web form, email or through the Blue Book directory — lands as unstructured text that one Senior Estimator and the office manager must personally read, qualify, chase for missing details and turn into a scoped estimate. The company has grown to 48 staff and $10M+ revenue with a single named Senior Estimator and a single office manager, and its stated growth targets (data-center/IT, pharmaceutical, warehousing) are exactly the segments that issue formal bid packages with drawings, specs and deadlines.
evidence: The company highlights hiring its first full-time Estimator in 2018 and now cites one Senior Estimator (John Hartnett) alongside one Office Manager (Maryann Budzin) for a 48-person firm — https://www.amecelectric.com/assets/docs/creating-connections.pdf

The web form collects only free-text project details and the site states AMEC will review the request and follow up with service, scheduling or quote information — every request passes through a human before any scoped response — https://www.amecelectric.com/free-consultation

Blue Book Network directory presence is linked from the site footer and the owner credits it as a growth source, i.e. bids arrive through a directory rather than a bid-management workflow — https://www.amecelectric.com/assets/docs/creating-connections.pdf
Owner-stated growth intent into IT/data-center, pharmaceutical and storage/warehousing segments, which are bid- and spec-driven — https://www.amecelectric.com/assets/docs/creating-connections.pdf
Preliminary cost estimates and business recordkeeping are documented as core electrician tasks, i.e. the estimating burden falls on trade staff — https://www.onetonline.org/link/summary/47-2111.00
Estimating/record-keeping workload is anchored to a real NJ wage: electricians median $77,250 statewide (2025 OEWS) — https://api.bls.gov/publicAPI/v1/timeseries/data/OEUS340000000000047211113
opportunities.agent_design: A pipeline of three cooperating agents with one human gate. (1) Intake agent watches the web-form endpoint and a shared estimating inbox, de-duplicates, and extracts client, site, scope type, drawing/spec attachments, due date and decision-maker into a structured request record. (2) Qualification agent checks the request against AMEC's actual capability list and service radius, flags missing information, and auto-drafts a specific clarification email to the client for the estimator to approve and send — rather than the estimator typing it. (3) Prep agent produces an estimate worksheet: scope line items from the request and attachments, a materials/labor checklist pulled from prior similar jobs in their ticket history, and a list of open questions, delivered to the Senior Estimator as a draft. Systems touched: email, web form, file storage (drawings/specs), prior-job history, and optionally the Blue Book/directory bid notices for discovery. Human approval: the Senior Estimator signs off on every number and every outbound clarification or proposal; the agent never sends a price. Every draft keeps its source citations so the estimator can audit where a line item came from.
opportunities.why_not_DIY: Generic chat assistants cannot read a drawing set or spec book, cannot retrieve comparable past jobs with their actual labor hours, and cannot hold a multi-week bid pipeline with deadlines. The value comes from retrieval over AMEC's own job history plus deterministic extraction and a bid calendar — integration into the ticket/estimating data, document parsing for drawings and specs, and a defensible audit trail. A wrong line item in a commercial electrical bid is a five- or six-figure mistake, so approval routing, versioning and diff-review are engineering requirements, not prompt tweaks.

impact_estimate.range: $14,000–$38,000/yr of recovered estimator/supervisor capacity; bid-win-rate uplift left unquantified
impact_estimate.assumptions: Assumes the estimator plus office manager spend roughly 8–15 hrs/week combined on reading raw requests, chasing missing scope details and re-keying them (inference from a single-estimator desk handling all inbound requests; no time study exists). Valued at $50.73–$77.25/hr (NJ medians for first-line construction supervisors $105,510 and electricians $77,250) → 400–780 hrs/yr. Pilot assumed to remove 35–50% of that clerical/prep share → $14k–$38k. Explicitly not claimed: more jobs won. That depends on hit rate and average ticket, neither of which is public; the brief found no measured NJ contractor evidence for booked-job uplift.

opportunities.pilot_scope: 2–4 weeks: run the intake + qualification agents over 4–6 weeks of historical web-form requests and estimating emails to measure how many were missing critical fields; build the clarification-draft and estimate-worksheet outputs for one service line (start with generators/UPS or lighting retrofit, both repeatable and common in their portfolio); have the Senior Estimator grade 15–20 drafts against his own quotes; deliver a comparison report plus a working intake inbox and bid calendar.

opportunities.title: Field Records & Job-Costing Integration Layer (with a client status view for uptime-critical accounts)
opportunities.problem: The back office has been built by hand: an office manager assembled a computerized work-ticket tool and digital time sheets, field crews report through iPads or phones, and employee documents (paystubs, forms) sit behind a single shared password. Nothing visible ties a ticket to labor hours, materials, warranty photos and a job-cost number, and clients in server rooms, refrigerated warehouses and dealerships have no portal to see ticket status or history — so status is answered by phone, and job-cost leakage (unbilled extra work, warranty callbacks) is only found later, if at all.
evidence: Office manager built the computerized work ticket and digital time sheets in-house; field crews use iPad, computer or company iPhone — homegrown tools, no named field-service platform — https://www.amecelectric.com/assets/docs/creating-connections.pdf

Employee self-service is an employees-only page protected by a single shared team password for paystubs, forms and company documents, indicating manual HR document handling and no per-user audit trail — https://www.amecelectric.com/employees
No customer portal or login exists anywhere on the public site; the only client-facing path is the consultation form and the main phone number — https://www.amecelectric.com/free-consultation

Recording time, materials and deficiencies on work orders and keeping repair records is a documented core task for the trades technicians AMEC employs — https://www.onetonline.org/link/summary/49-9021.00

Named client segments are uptime-sensitive (server manufacturers, refrigerated warehouses, food processing, car dealerships), where downtime and documentation matter to the client — https://www.amecelectric.com/assets/docs/creating-connections.pdf
Electricians in NJ earn a median $77,250 (2025 OEWS), so every unbilled or re-keyed field hour is expensive — https://api.bls.gov/publicAPI/v1/timeseries/data/OEUS340000000000047211113
opportunities.agent_design: An agent-built integration layer plus two lightweight front ends. Agent 1 (records agent) turns a technician's voice note, photos or short text at job close into a structured work-order record — work performed, materials used, deficiency found, next action, warranty flag — written back into the existing ticket tool so the homegrown system is kept, not replaced. Agent 2 (costing agent) joins daily time-sheet entries to tickets weekly and produces a per-job margin view, flagging tickets with no billed labor, overtime, or a deficiency note with no follow-up quote attached. Agent 3 (client status agent) generates a per-account service history page and a weekly ticket-status summary email, optionally behind a named-user portal. Systems touched: the internal work-ticket tool, digital time-sheet export, accounting (QuickBooks presumed, unconfirmed — to be verified), photo storage, and email. Human approval: the office manager approves any record written back and any flag before it reaches billing or a client; the GM of Operations approves cost views leaving the building. Named-user access replaces the shared-password page as a security prerequisite for any client-facing view.
opportunities.why_not_DIY: The core work is integration and data modeling across tools that were never designed to talk (a hand-built ticket tool, a time-sheet export, accounting, photo storage), with write-back into a system that has no public API. Off-the-shelf AI note-takers produce pretty summaries but do not reconcile a timesheet to a ticket, do not know which deficiency note became an unbilled change order, and cannot expose client data safely behind a shared password. Turning the shared-password page into named users is a security change, not a content change — and it is the gate on everything client-facing.

impact_estimate.range: $22,000–$55,000/yr of recovered field and office time; unbilled-change-order recovery left out of the range
impact_estimate.assumptions: Assumes 48 field and supervisory staff average 20–30 min/day on paperwork and re-keying (ticket notes, timesheets, warranty documentation), roughly 250 workdays → 4,000–6,000 hrs/yr. Valued at the NJ electrician median $77,250/yr ≈ $37.14/hr → $148k–$223k at full rate. Pilot assumed to remove 15–25% of that clerical share → $22k–$55k, with the office manager's review time counted as a cost against it. Excluded from the range: recovered unbilled change orders and avoided warranty callbacks, because no benchmark for leakage rate in electrical contracting was located in this run — that upside is an unquantified inference.

opportunities.pilot_scope: 2–4 weeks on one crew and one client segment (recommend the auto-dealership or refrigeration accounts, which generate repeat tickets): map the existing ticket and time-sheet data, ship the structured work-order record with office-manager approval, stand up the weekly per-job margin report, and deliver a read-only per-account service history page for two named client contacts. Explicitly out of scope for the pilot: replacing the existing ticket system, payroll changes, and any client-facing login until named-user authentication is agreed.

lead_score.rationale: Pain (18/30): the operational signals are structural and consistent — 24/7 service on rotating on-call duty behind one phone number, a single Senior Estimator for all inbound quoting, homegrown work-ticket tools, and a shared-password employee page — but no complaint, response-time or job-posting evidence could be sourced (Google/Yelp/BBB/Indeed all blocked, LinkedIn 403), so pain is inferred from company statements rather than measured in customer outcomes. Fit (17/20): the three highest-value problems are textbook capability-A intake/dispatch/quoting work plus one capability-D integration, all in AMEC's own described workflow, with no hardware required. Ability to pay (15/20): $10M+ revenue, 48 full-time staff, capital-project and uptime-critical clients give real budget headroom, but the company's own numbers suggest revenue is flat or below its 2020 peak ($12M+ cited for 2020 vs '$10 million+' for 2025), which argues for a mid-five-figure pilot rather than a large program. Ease (10/15): a single Metuchen site, a named founder/President and a named GM of Operations make decision-making short, and one phone line plus one web form is a contained pilot surface; deductions for a founder-led contractor culture with almost no visible technology adoption (blog dormant since Aug 2022, no careers page, no booking, no portal) and for an unknown internal stack — whether they run QuickBooks, ServiceTitan or nothing at all is undisclosed, and that discovery is a real pilot risk. Strategic (12/15): the design patterns (after-hours intake, RFQ-to-estimate prep, field-record integration) port directly to other NJ commercial trade contractors with 20–100 staff, a highly repeatable archetype, though the firm is not itself a multi-site reference account. Evidence thin: revenue figures conflict across sources and no internal systems, call volumes or quote volumes are public; the impact ranges lean on BLS wage medians and on an analogue study from customer-support work, not on measured contractor outcomes.

best_evidence_signal: 24/7 breakdown service for uptime-critical clients is run on rotating on-call duty behind a single main phone number with no after-hours web path or dispatch system — https://www.amecelectric.com/assets/docs/creating-connections.pdf
suggested_channel: email to Brian Schnaak, General Manager of Operations (operations owner, gatekeeper for dispatch and the office manager), referencing the 24/7 service; walk-in to the Liberty Street shop as the follow-up if email goes unanswered
